readings.title: Our Hero
readings.challenge: Notice what a speaker confesses about herself while praising someone else.
readings.focus: Passengers on a burning steamboat are saved by a man whose people they had despised.
readings.context: Frances Ellen Watkins Harper (1825–1911) was born free in Baltimore, Maryland, while slavery was still legal there. She became a famous speaker against slavery and for women’s rights, and one of the best-known African American poets of her century. Atlanta Offering: Poems appeared in 1895. The speaker is a passenger on a burning steamboat, the Hannah. Harper does not name the hero; the lines about his “race” and “darkened face” suggest he is Black and the passengers are not. Consternation is sudden alarm; the pilot steers the boat with the rudder; the keel is its bottom; a martyr is someone who dies for others.
readings.contentNote: A man dies in a fire after saving the passengers, who admit they once despised his race.

excerpt.locator: Atlanta Offering, “Our Hero,” the whole poem; opens “ Onward to her destination, O'er the stream the Hannah sped, When a cry of consternation…”; closes “…crimson fields of strife, Grander, nobler, than that pilot Yielding up for us his life.”.

questions.prompt: What goes wrong on the Hannah, and why does the pilot’s flight make it worse?
facilitatorNotes: Fire breaks out, and the pilot who should steer runs for his life, so the boat drifts helplessly with no one at the rudder.
evidence: When we saw the pilot flying,
Helplessly the boat was drifting,

questions.prompt: “We had once despised his race.” What does this line tell you about the speaker, and why does Harper put it just before the rescue?
facilitatorNotes: The passengers looked down on the man’s people. The person they despised is the one who saves them, so his courage exposes their prejudice. Harper lets the passengers confess it themselves.
evidence: We had once despised his race--
But we saw a lofty purpose

questions.prompt: One stanza is made only of questions. What effect do they have?
facilitatorNotes: They put the reader inside the passengers’ breathless waiting: can he do it, and will he give his life? The answer is held back for two more stanzas.
evidence: Could he save us? Would he save us?
Breathlessly we watched and waited

questions.prompt: Why does Harper say no hero of the battlefield was grander than this pilot?
facilitatorNotes: Soldiers win fame by fighting; he gave his life to save others, with no fame to gain. Readers may debate whether one kind of courage is greater than another.
evidence: Fame has never crowned a hero
Yielding up for us his life.

readings.title: The Dying Bondman
readings.challenge: Work out why a written word matters so much to a man at the end of his life.
readings.focus: An enslaved man, once a free African leader, asks to die free.
readings.context: Frances Ellen Watkins Harper (1825–1911) was born free in Baltimore, Maryland, while slavery was still legal there. She became a famous speaker against slavery and for women’s rights, and one of the best-known African American poets of her century. Atlanta Offering: Poems appeared in 1895. A bondman is an enslaved man; slavery ended in the United States in 1865. Afric means African; a chieftain is a leader; “life’s sands were almost run” compares a life to sand running out of an hourglass; wan means pale; a token is a sign or proof.
readings.contentNote: The poem is about slavery: a man captured in war dies still enslaved until his last moment.

excerpt.locator: Atlanta Offering, “The Dying Bondman,” the whole poem; opens “ Life was trembling, faintly trembling On the bondman's latest breath, And he felt the…”; closes “…"I am free!" at last he said. Backward fell upon the pillow, He was free among the dead.”.

questions.prompt: Who had the bondman been before he was enslaved? Why does the poem tell us?
facilitatorNotes: An African chieftain who wore his manhood “as a crown” until he was struck down in battle. His past shows how much slavery took from him.
evidence: He had been an Afric chieftain,
Worn his manhood as a crown;

questions.prompt: He is about to die. Why does he still want his freedom written down?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to meet his ancestors as a free man; he believes their spirits would “shrink back” from one who lived and died a slave. Freedom matters to him as honour, not only as a way to live.
evidence: I a slave had lived and died;
That my kindred dead may see--

questions.prompt: What does the master’s action show: kindness, or too little too late?
facilitatorNotes: He writes the release at once when asked. But he could have freed the man at any time, and the man had “hoped in vain” for years. Readers can weigh both.
evidence: Wrote for him the glad release,
Waited, watched and hoped in vain,

questions.prompt: The last line is “He was free among the dead.” Is the ending happy, sad, or both?
facilitatorNotes: He dies at peace, with “one sweet smile,” holding his freedom; yet freedom came only at death. The line can be read as a triumph and as an accusation against slavery.
evidence: Flitted one sweet smile of peace.
He was free among the dead.

readings.title: Home, Sweet Home
readings.challenge: Notice how a shared feeling can join people who are fighting, and for how long.
readings.focus: Two enemy camps stop singing their own songs and join in one about home.
readings.context: Frances Ellen Watkins Harper (1825–1911) was born free in Baltimore, Maryland, while slavery was still legal there. She became a famous speaker against slavery and for women’s rights, and one of the best-known African American poets of her century. Atlanta Offering: Poems appeared in 1895. The poem recalls a story told about the Civil War (1861–1865): Union and Confederate armies camped on opposite banks of a river, their bands played rival songs, and then both joined in the old song “Home, Sweet Home.” “Dixie” was the Confederate South’s song; the banner “Waved so long from strand to strand” is the American flag of “The Star-Spangled Banner.” Even means evening; carnage is slaughter; an ensign is a flag.

excerpt.locator: Atlanta Offering, “Home, Sweet Home,” the whole poem; opens “ Sharers of a common country, They had met in deadly strife; Men who should have been as…”; closes “…land from shore to shore, But may mother, home and Heaven, Be our watchwords evermore.”.

questions.prompt: What is each camp singing at first, and what does each song stand for?
facilitatorNotes: One sings “Dixie,” the South; the other sings of the flag, the Union. Harper adds that where Dixie’s flag flew, enslaved people hoped for the Union’s banner of freedom.
evidence: Down in Dixie, Dixie's land,
Floated o'er the hopeful slave,

questions.prompt: What happens when “Home, Sweet Home” begins? Which words show the change?
facilitatorNotes: Strong men’s hearts melt, the two camps sing one chorus, and for a while they are “only brothers.” Being soldiers gives way to being men who miss home.
evidence: They were only brothers then,
Not as soldiers, but as men.

questions.prompt: “That touch of nature” comes from Shakespeare: “One touch of nature makes the whole world kin.” How does the song prove this? Does the poem show its limits too?
facilitatorNotes: Missing home is a feeling both sides share, and it makes them kin. But it lasts only “for awhile,” and the poem ends with a prayer that war never come again. Readers may say whether a shared feeling can stop a war.
evidence: Telling us we all are kin.
For awhile, all strife forgotten,

readings.title: Death of the Old Sea King
readings.challenge: Hear how a storm and a death are made to match each other.
readings.focus: A dying Viking chief hears his god’s call in the storm and goes to meet it.
readings.context: Frances Ellen Watkins Harper (1825–1911) was born free in Baltimore, Maryland, while slavery was still legal there. She became a famous speaker against slavery and for women’s rights, and one of the best-known African American poets of her century. Atlanta Offering: Poems appeared in 1895. This poem imagines the death of a Viking chief, a sea-king. In Norse myth Odin was the chief god, and the Valkyrs (Valkyries) were warrior maidens who carried brave fighters to his hall; some Viking chiefs were given funerals on burning ships. A pyre is a pile of wood for burning; fitful means stormy and changing.
readings.contentNote: At his own command, the dying chief is carried onto his ship and burned on it.

excerpt.locator: Atlanta Offering, “Death of the Old Sea King,” the whole poem; opens “ 'Twas a fearful night--the tempest raved With loud and wrathful pride, The storm-king…”; closes “…men held their breath, The brave old man went boldly forth And calmly talked with death.”.

questions.prompt: How does the storm change the dying sea-king?
facilitatorNotes: His hearing was failing, but the storm stirs his “sluggish blood” and fills his eyes with light; he hears Odin’s call in the tempest.
evidence: With sudden vigor stirred.
His eyes grew full of light;

questions.prompt: What does he ask his men to do, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Bring his robes, sword and armour, carry him to his best ship and light a funeral pyre, so that he goes to Odin’s hall as a warrior rather than dying in bed.
evidence: Now bring me here my warrior robes,
Light up a funeral pyre;

questions.prompt: How does Harper make this death seem brave rather than only sad?
facilitatorNotes: The flames are like a banner; there is no cry of pain; the watchers hold their breath while he “calmly talked with death.” Some readers will find it noble, others frightening. The poem shows what he believed without asking us to share it.
evidence: But they heard no cry of anguish
And calmly talked with death.

readings.title: Vashti
readings.challenge: Compare the motives of a king, a queen and the king’s advisers.
readings.focus: A queen refuses to be shown off, and loses her crown rather than her dignity.
readings.context: Frances Ellen Watkins Harper (1825–1911) was born free in Baltimore, Maryland, while slavery was still legal there. She became a famous speaker against slavery and for women’s rights, and one of the best-known African American poets of her century. Atlanta Offering: Poems appeared in 1895. Harper retells a story from the Bible’s Book of Esther. The king of Persia, feasting with his lords, ordered Queen Vashti to come and show her beauty to them; a Persian queen did not show her face to crowds of men. A decree is an order; chamberlains are palace officers; counsellors give advice; Ind is India and Ethiop is Ethiopia; restive means restless and hard to control.

excerpt.locator: Atlanta Offering, “Vashti,” the whole poem; opens “ She leaned her head upon her hand And heard the King's decree-- "My lords are feasting…”; closes “…Proud of her spotless name-- A woman who could bend to grief, But would not bow to shame.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the King want Vashti to come? What does the way he speaks of her suggest?
facilitatorNotes: He has already shown his lords his treasures and jewels, and now wants to show her. Calling her “my beautiful, my own” and comparing her with gems suggests he treats her as one more possession.
evidence: I've shown the treasures of my house,
My beautiful, my own!

questions.prompt: Why does Vashti refuse? Find two reasons in her answer.
facilitatorNotes: She is Persia’s Queen, not a show for “merry men,” and being unveiled before a crowd would shame her and all Persian women. She would rather lose her crown, or die.
evidence: That I am Persia's Queen,
That I would rather die.

questions.prompt: What are the counsellors really afraid of?
facilitatorNotes: Not Vashti herself, but that other women would see her disobey and “learn to scorn our name.” They want her punished as a warning. Harper calls them “wily,” which shows what she thinks of them.
evidence: The women, restive 'neath our rule,
Then spake his wily counsellors--

questions.prompt: Vashti “could bend to grief, / But would not bow to shame.” Did she win or lose?
facilitatorNotes: She loses her crown and her palace but keeps her “spotless name,” and the poem honours her strength. Readers may weigh whether the cost was worth it.
evidence: Proud of her spotless name--
But would not bow to shame.
